title: Faith Under Persecution
subtitle: The Trials of the Vulnerable and the First Martyrs of Islam
summary: The shift from verbal opposition to physical torture in Makkah, the targeting of the vulnerable believers (Al-Mustad'afun), the ordeal and martyrdom of the Family of Yasir, the trial of Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, the spiritual meaning of steadfast patience (sabr), and divine solace in the Quran.

sections.text: The Shift to Systematic Torture

When diplomatic ultimatums, offers of bribery, and propaganda campaigns failed to halt the spread of Islam, the chieftains of Quraysh unleashed brutal physical repression. Because influential converts belonging to powerful clans—such as Abu Bakr of Banu Taym or 'Uthman of Banu Umayyah—enjoyed some degree of tribal deterrence, persecution fell with savage fury upon the most vulnerable believers (*Al-Mustad'afun*): enslaved men and women, foreign residents, and allied clients who possessed no tribal lineage to shield them.

Ibn Ishaq relates that each clan set upon those of its own members who had become Muslims, imprisoning them, beating them, depriving them of food and drink, and exposing them to the heat of Makkah to turn them from their religion. A report of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud in Sunan Ibn Majah names seven who were the first to show their Islam openly: the Prophet, Abu Bakr, 'Ammar, his mother Sumayyah, Suhayb, Bilal and al-Miqdad. God protected the Prophet through his uncle Abu Talib and Abu Bakr through his people; the rest were seized by the polytheists.
The scorching desert plains of al-Batha outside Makkah where vulnerable believers were tormented.
The Ordeal of the Family of Yasir

Among the most harrowing accounts in early Islamic history is the ordeal of the family of Yasir. Yasir ibn 'Amir had come to Makkah from Yemen and become an ally of the clan of Banu Makhzum. He married Sumayyah bint Khayyat, a slave woman of that clan, and they had a son, 'Ammar. When the family embraced Islam, Ibn Ishaq relates, Banu Makhzum would take them out into the heat of Makkah and torture them; Abu Jahl is named in the reports as foremost among their tormentors.
In the report of Ibn Mas'ud in Sunan Ibn Majah, the polytheists dressed those they seized in coats of iron mail and left them to bake in the sun.

Ibn Ishaq relates that the Prophet ﷺ would pass by them while they were being tortured and, unable to protect them, would say: 'Patience, O family of Yasir! Your appointed meeting place is Paradise.' The report is also transmitted by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak; scholars differ over its chains, and some consider it sound through its supporting narrations.
"Patience, O family of Yasir! Your appointed meeting place is Paradise." — Ibn Ishaq, in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham; al-Hakim, al-Mustadrak
The First Martyr of Islam

Sirah reports relate that Abu Jahl killed Sumayyah with a spear, and she is remembered as the first martyr (shahidah) in Islam. The report of Ibn Mas'ud in Sunan Ibn Majah states, however, that all of those tortured except Bilal eventually said what their tormentors demanded of them. The two accounts are not easily reconciled; the Qur'an, as described below, excuses words spoken under coercion while the heart remains firm in faith.

Sirah reports add that Yasir also died under the torture. 'Ammar survived, but reports in the commentaries on the Qur'an relate that under severe torment he spoke the words his tormentors demanded, and then came to the Prophet in distress, fearing for his faith.

In a report transmitted by al-Hakim and by commentators such as al-Tabari, whose chain is disconnected, the Prophet asked him: 'How do you find your heart?' He replied: 'Content with faith.' The Prophet said: 'If they do it again, then do the same.' Commentators connect this incident with the verse of Surah An-Nahl: 'except for one who is forced while his heart is content with faith' (16:106).
The Steadfastness of Khabbab ibn al-Aratt

Another example of endurance was Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, a blacksmith. He had been taken captive as a child and sold in Makkah; the sources name his owner as Siba' ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza al-Khuza'i or as Umm Anmar, of the same family. He was among the earliest Muslims. Classical biographical works relate that the polytheists seized him and tortured him severely: they would strip him and press his back against hot pebbles and then against heated stones, and twist his head, but he did not give them what they wanted.

A report transmitted from Abu Layla al-Kindi relates that years later Khabbab came to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who seated him on his own cushion and said that no one was more entitled to that seat except Bilal. Khabbab replied that Bilal had at least had someone among the polytheists through whom God protected him, while he had had no one. He described how one day they lit a fire for him and laid him on it while a man pressed his foot on his chest, so that only his back lay between him and the ground. Then he uncovered his back, and it was marked with white scars.

Khabbab himself described in Sahih al-Bukhari how, during these years, he came to the Prophet seeking his prayer for the persecuted believers. The Prophet was reclining on his cloak in the shade of the Kaaba. He sat up, his face red, and reminded Khabbab of the believers of earlier times, then gave a promise for the future:

"Among those before you, a man's flesh and sinews would be combed from his bones with combs of iron, and that would not turn him from his religion; a saw would be placed on the parting of his head and he would be split in two, and that would not turn him from his religion. God will surely complete this matter, until a rider travels from San'a' to Hadramawt fearing none but God." — Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 3852
The silent stars over the desert night, solace to those enduring persecution for the sake of God.
The Spiritual Meaning of Sabr and Divine Promise

During these years of persecution, Qur'anic revelation strengthened the believers' resolve and taught them that trials were a way by which God tests sincerity. Patience (sabr) was presented not as passive surrender but as firm endurance in the path of truth.

﴿أَحَسِبَ النَّاسُ أَن يُتْرَكُوا أَن يَقُولُوا آمَنَّا وَهُمْ لَا يُفْتَنُونَ ۝ وَلَقَدْ فَتَنَّا الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ ۖ فَلَيَعْلَمَنَّ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ صَدَقُوا وَلَيَعْلَمَنَّ الْكَاذِبِينَ﴾

"Do the people think that they will be left to say, 'We believe' and they will not be tried? But We have certainly tried those before them, and Allah will surely make evident those who are truthful, and He will surely make evident the liars." — Surah Al-Ankabut (29:2–3)
The steadfastness of these early believers, most of them people without wealth or tribal protection, became one of the defining memories of the Makkan period.
